title.narrative: Multi-Hazard Assessments for Building Sustainable and Resilient Communities

description.narrative:
Considerable ambiguity surrounds the likely impacts of climate change; this presents major challenges especially in multi-hazard environments where humanitarian and development practitioners have to decide how and where to allocate resources in order to reduce disaster risk and promote long-term sustainable development. In recent years, climate change has become the focus of attention for many in the humanitarian and development sectors – it is seen to be the ‘most serious and urgent problem the world faces’. Whilst globally, this view may be valid, at a local scale, other environmental hazards and human induced environmental degradation are often far more damaging and, currently, have much greater impact on communities and livelihoods than climate change alone. This is particularly the case in many developing countries where humanitarian and development practitioners must target their resources responsibly and sustainably.
Whilst this research will not attempt to play down the important threat climate change poses to human security, it will aim to develop methodologies which will allow multi-hazard assessments to be undertaken. These will allow humanitarian and development practitioners the opportunity to analyse threats to human security, the vulnerability of communities to such threats and their capacity to deal with them. This will subsequently lead to the development of tools to enable the effective application of indigenous and scientific knowledge to build resilience.
Importantly this research will allow the threat of climate change to be analysed in the context of other threats to ensure undue attention is not focused on the issue unless there is reason to do so. In order to achieve this challenging undertaking, environmental hazards, including climate change, will be appropriately assessed and the associated risks mapped and quantified in order to set a priority agenda for disaster risk reduction (DRR) and adaptation to climate change.
Whilst this research will have global applicability through the provision of new methodological approaches for the humanitarian and development sectors, it will also be of great value at the community level. Importantly, indigenous knowledge will be recognised as a community resource and a building block in developing community resilience to environmental hazards. In order to ‘ground’ the research, field work will be carried out in a multi-hazard environment (the Philippines) which presents unique challenges and opportunities for work in the fields of DRR and climate change adaptation.
This EngD project aims to show how the humanitarian and development sector can usefully assess hazards and prioritise their work in multi-hazard environments. It aims to provide a way for helping communities build resilience to the threats that are most likely to undermine their security both now and in the future, through utilising both scientific and indigenous knowledge.
